issue_context.title: `change_scene_to()` fails silently when provided a `Node`
issue_context.body:
### Godot version

3.5.rc7

### System information

Linux Mint 20.3

### Issue description

Running `change_scene_to()` with an object that is not a `PackedScene` seems to cause the method to fail silently - it reports `0` and deletes the `current_scene` but does not replace the active scene, from checking the scene tree or any subsequent code in `_ready()` on the new scene. Tested with a new `Node2D` as well as a `PackedScene` with `instance()` called on it (which might be closer to something somebody might inadvertently do when coding normally)

### Steps to reproduce

```
var my_scene = load("res://my_scene.tscn").instance()
get_tree().change_scene_to(my_scene)
```
can also be done with a new copy of a node
```
get_tree().change_scene(Node2D.new())
```

### Minimal reproduction project

[changescenetest.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/9205608/changescenetest.zip)
comments:
Calling `change_scene()` with `Node2D.new()` generates a parser error for me:

> At "change_scene_to()" call, argument 1. The passed argument's type (Node2D) doesn't match the function's expected argument type (PackedScene).

For the first case, it's equivalent to `change_scene(null)` which unloads current scene. e.g. You can do this from an Autoload.

Ah, you're correct - I compressed my example from
```
var node = Node2D.new()
get_tree().change_scene(node)
```
down to one line but I should have realized that would be behavior more in line with the first example.

That being said, *should* that behavior in the first example just silently be treated as `change_scene(null)`? That feels pretty clearly like that's not what a person would intend when they write those two lines. If the program ends up continuing, that's one thing, but I feel like there should be some kind of engine notification (`Warning: calling "instance()" on type x provided null object` or something similar). As it stands right now, nothing happens, which can be confusing behavior.

That's the dynamic typing nature of GDScript. You can use [static typing](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/scripting/gdscript/static_typing.html) if you want this kind of error.

```gdscript
# This prints "null"
var foo = Node2D.new()
var bar = foo as PackedScene
print(bar)

# This results in an invalid cast error
var foo := Node2D.new()
var bar := foo as PackedScene
print(bar)
```

Sure, I get that the type cannot be determined by the interpreter - my issue is more with the fact that there's no notice to the user that it's being treated as `null`. I guess, to go a little further, I'm not sure why that should be acceptable behavior at all when you can `get_tree().get_root().remove_child()` on `current_scene`. That has an explicitness to it which suggests that the user *wants* it to happen, while `get_tree().change_scene_to(null)` feels like magic behavior since we're only using half of a function's purpose to achieve something that is not described within documents. Then, to compound to that issue, items are automatically cast to null when they do not fit the expected type. Even if this is intended behavior, there's no notice to the user at all or documentation to suggest that this is possible, which causes uncertainty.

For 4.0, I agree using a `null` argument should cause an error message to be printed. Unloading the current scene should be done with a method that should be added, e.g. `unload_current_scene()` (like `reload_current_scene()`).

For 3.x, I think the only thing we can do is improve the documentation.
